reflection.title: Reflection
reflection.body:
Southeast Asia is home to more than 1,200 bird species and is part of one of the world's great avian migratory routes: the East Asian–Australasian Flyway, which links tropical, temperate and Arctic landscapes. 
Birds have long shared Southeast Asia's forests, wetlands, rice fields, mangroves, estuaries and coasts with the peoples of the region. Over millennia, birds came to symbolize beauty, wisdom, courage, discernment, prosperity, protection and spiritual power, as recorded in stories, scripture and legends. In the Vattaka Jataka, a young quail overcomes a wildfire through the power of virtue, becoming a symbol of protection and loving-kindness throughout the Theravada Buddhist world. Hindu traditions portray birds as the divine mounts (vahana) of the gods, including the peacock of Kartikeya and the hamsa of Brahma and Saraswati. Similarly, Islamic traditions portray birds as celestial messengers and examples of trust in the divine. In Iban tradition, Sengalang Burong, the god of war, communicates with humans through omen birds and has the earthly form of the Brahminy kite. 
The objects presented in this trail reveal how communities have incorporated birds into everyday life, rituals, ceremonies and art. The quail of the Vattaka Jataka appears on a silver casket used for betel sharing, connecting Buddhist teachings with the social traditions of Malay and Thai communities. In Brunei, a bird from the paddy fields decorates the handle of a copper betel cutter, while Peranakan belt buckles include birds as symbols of protection and prosperity. 
These objects convey how birds are part of both ecosystems and imagination, everyday life and ritual, carrying meanings that communities express in their artistic traditions and material cultures. In doing so, birds connect landscapes and communities across Southeast Asia.

reflection.title: Reflection
reflection.body:
Recognizable by their large bills and distinctive casque, hornbills inhabit the tropical forests of Southeast Asia where they depend on mature trees for nesting and fruiting forests for food. As important seed dispersers, they help sustain the forest ecosystems that have sustained communities across Southeast Asia for generations. 
The striking appearance, distinctive calls and habits of hornbills have resonated with the people of the region who have incorporated hornbills into indigenous knowledge, ritual practices and visual culture over millennia. Representations of hornbills appear in rock art from Kalimantan, on Neolithic earthenware from Sarawak and on Đông Sơn bronze drums from Viet Nam. 
The hornbill is admired across Southeast Asia, but nowhere is this bird more deeply woven into community life than among the Dayak peoples of Borneo, particularly the Iban and the Orang Ulu. Among the Iban, hornbills are regarded as sacred beings, bearers of good omens and intermediaries between the human and spirit worlds. Among the Orang Ulu, they also express ancestry, prestige and social standing. Reading the calls and flight paths of birds was historically a sacred practice that guided major decisions, from clearing land for cultivation to preparing for war. 
These relationships are embodied in the stories of Sengalang Burong, the Iban deity of the spirit world, warfare and divination. Although Sengalang Burong takes the form of a Brahminy kite, he is closely connected to hornbills as these birds carry messages between the divine and human worlds. During the Gawai Burong festival, communities honour Sengalang Burong by carving and raising monumental kenyalang statues that provide protection, health and prosperity for the community.
The objects in this trail reveal how hornbills continue to connect forests, ritual and communities. Hornbill motifs were incorporated into calapa containers, sulang vessels, weapons and tools such as the badau, and hornbill skulls and feathers were elements of the katapu (war helmet). 
Together, these objects show how the traditional knowledge of communities, gained through close observation of the natural world, was transformed into enduring artistic, ceremonial and material traditions. Today, the hornbill continues to connect forest life, spiritual practices and communities across Borneo while contributing to Southeast Asia's shared heritage.

reflection.title: Reflection
reflection.body:
Waterbirds are a significant feature of Southeast Asia's rivers, wetlands, floodplains, estuaries, mangroves and coasts, and these birds, including kingfishers, cranes, geese, ducks and egrets, are essential for the functioning of these aquatic ecosystems. 
Over millennia, the communities living alongside these birds came to associate them with grace, longevity, wisdom, vigilance, keen observation, harmony, abundance and prosperity, and this association found expression in diverse cultural traditions. 
In Hindu mythology the hamsa or hintha (a goose, swan or waterbird) is known as the vahana (mount or vehicle) of Brahma and Saraswati. The mythical hamsa is celebrated in Hindu lore for its legendary capacity to separate milk from water, and in particular drink only the milk while leaving behind the water, representing discernment and the ability to differentiate truth from illusion. 
Among Lanna and Mon communities, the hintha became an enduring cultural emblem associated with purity, prosperity and community identity. According to Mon tradition, the Buddha foretold the founding of Bago (Hanthawaddy) after seeing two hintha resting on a single rock rising from the sea. 
Along the east coast of the Malay Peninsula, fishing communities perceive the bangau (stork) as possessing a semangat (spirit) that protects boats at sea. Traditional kolek and kolae boats are carved with bangau and anak bangau figures on their prows, reflecting the bird's associations with patience, vigilance and safe return. These practices form part of maritime traditions shared by communities in Peninsular Malaysia and southern Thailand.
The objects in this trail reveal how communities have incorporated waterbirds into artistic, ceremonial and everyday life. Egret imagery on Đông Sơn bronze drums reflects the importance of wetlands and seasonal cycles. Hamsa-shaped vessels hold consecrated water used in Hindu-Buddhist ceremonies, while cranes on Ming blue-and-white porcelain and Baba & Nyonya ornaments express wishes for longevity, harmony and prosperity. A kingfisher-shaped keris hilt reflects artistic traditions shared between Kelantan and Pattani.
Through these diverse objects, communities wove the qualities of waterbirds into rituals, artisanship and daily life. Living in and along the wetlands and waterways that sustain Southeast Asia, waterbirds continue to connect ecosystems, livelihoods and cultural traditions across the region.

reflection.title: Reflection
reflection.body:
Genetic and archaeological studies trace the domestic chicken's primary ancestor to the Southeast Asian red junglefowl (Gallus gallus spadiceus). Over millennia, junglefowl gradually became a permanent part of human settlements, transforming into chickens and merging with the daily rhythms of food production, farming and household life.
As one of Southeast Asia's oldest domesticated animals, chickens acquired rich cultural meanings and became part of ritual and ceremonial life across the region. Across Malay, Thai, Chinese, Peranakan, Hindu-Buddhist and Muslim traditions, the chicken is far more than a domestic animal; it has symbolic associations, embodying prosperity, fertility and renewal. 
In mainland Southeast Asia, chickens appear in spirit-house offerings and practices connected with guardianship and the unseen world. The rooster’s crow heralds the beginning of a new day, linking it to ideas of time, order, renewal and protection. Roosters came to symbolize dawn, vigilance, courage and good fortune, while hens and chicks evoked nurture, continuity and household abundance.
Various cultures associate meanings with cockfighting. Among Iban communities of Sarawak, cockfighting (nyabong) is rooted in local mythology and ceremonial life, and sometimes a cockfight serves to resolve disputes. In Bali, the tabuh rah ceremony, a Hindu purification ritual, offers rooster blood to restore cosmic balance. 
The objects in this trail reveal the many ways chickens appear in Southeast Asia's material culture as  physical expressions of symbolic meanings. Roosters appear on zoomorphic tin ingots used in regional systems of exchange, ceremonial daggers such as the lawi ayam, rice-harvesting sickles and domestic and ceremonial vessels, including tempayan and sulang.

reflection.title: Reflection
reflection.body:
In the Hindu epic Ramayana, Garuda frees Rama and his brother from the serpent-arrows of their enemies. In Southeast Asia, where the relationship between birds and serpents was familiar, this story merged with regional traditions such as the Thai Ramakien, where Garuda likewise represents protection and victory over harmful forces.
Communities across Southeast Asia expressed such ideas through various forms of material culture. In Java and Bali, Garuda figures carrying Vishnu were placed in sacred spaces as guardians of the boundary between the earthly and the divine. On a southern Thai holy water basin, Garuda signifies supreme authority and protection against evil spirits. Garuda also became a national emblem in both Thailand and Indonesia. In Thailand's Trang Province, a master weaver adapted into her craft Garuda motifs that she observed on official buildings and temples. Thus, the bird also entered the textile traditions of village weavers. Today, the Garuda emblem spans various aspects of modern life, appearing on passports, official seals and even the name of a national airline.
Garuda is part of epic mythology and everyday life across Southeast Asia; a presence in sacred spaces, ritual objects and community traditions. Garuda does not carry a single fixed meaning, instead communities have interpreted the mythical bird to express protection, authority, devotion and identity in different ways. Through these diverse yet shared expressions, Garuda became an enduring thread in Southeast Asia's shared heritage.

reflection.title: Reflection
reflection.body:
The phoenix, which evokes qualities such as virtue, grace and refinement, entered Southeast Asia through trade and via the settlement of Chinese merchants and diaspora communities. Over time, communities across the region reinterpreted the symbolism of the creature and integrated it into ceremonial practice and everyday life.
Across Southeast Asia, the phoenix was depicted in ubiquitous representations. On a Peranakan kam cheng storage jar, the phoenix appears beside the peony, as an expression of wishes for a harmonious and prosperous household. On a batik cloth from Central Java, the burung hong (phoenix) is woven among Javanese floral motifs. As an image on a Vietnamese stoneware vessel, the phoenix elevates a functional jar to a gift worthy of diplomatic exchange. On a charcoal iron used to press wedding garments, the pairing of dragon and phoenix transforms a household object into a wish for marital harmony and prosperity. Through these diverse expressions, the phoenix became an enduring thread in Southeast Asia's shared heritage.

reflection.title: Reflection
reflection.body:
Centuries of engagement with Chinese traditions gave rise to distinctive dragon traditions in the cultures of many countries in Southeast Asia. In Viet Nam, for instance, origin stories trace the ancestry of the Vietnamese people to the union of dragon Lord Lạc Long Quân and Mountain Fairy Âu Cơ, a lineage that brought together the powers of water and land.
As Chinese merchant networks and diaspora communities carried dragon traditions along maritime routes to places such as Songkhla and Phuket, they encountered an older tradition of a mythical creature already established across Southeast Asia: the Naga. Although the Chinese long and the Southeast Asian Naga emerged from different cultural traditions, both were understood as guardians of water, rulers of rainfall and powerful protective beings.
Rather than replacing one another, these traditions came to be understood together. Communities recognized familiar meanings within new artistic forms, weaving the dragon into existing understandings of the natural and spiritual worlds while allowing older traditions to continue alongside it. 
The objects in this trail reveal these shared histories of exchange and reinterpretation. The Chinese-derived dragon motif became part of Malay courtly traditions via a royal court gong – bearing the image of a dragon – that announced the Sultan's decrees. A holy water vessel featuring dragon handles combines Chinese beliefs in the dragon’s protective powers with Theravada Buddhist ritual function. A dragon-shaped cannon incorporated Chinese design elements into Malay decorative art, demonstrating the creature's established association with protective and destructive power across different cultural worlds.
The dragon's enduring presence in Southeast Asia reflects a continuous process of cultural exchange and reinterpretation. Across the region, communities recognized the dragon's association with water, protection and the natural world, adapting it and incorporating it into local beliefs and artistic traditions.

reflection.title: Reflection
reflection.body:
As a symbol of strength, patience and fertility, the buffalo came to occupy an important place in stories, beliefs and ritual life. In Malay-Indonesian folklore, its strength provides a foil to the wit of the mouse deer (kancil). Hindu-Buddhist traditions associate the buffalo with powerful moral and cosmological themes: as Mahishasura, the buffalo demon defeated by the goddess Durga; as the vahana of Yama, the lord of death; and in Buddhist allegories such as the Mahisa Jataka, where it represents the patient mind seeking enlightenment.
Beyond these stories, the buffalo has long connected everyday life with ceremony. Across Southeast Asia, it features in agricultural rituals that bless the harvest, while among Toraja communities of Sulawesi, buffalo sacrifices remain central to burial ceremonies, marking ancestral passage, social status and collective memory.
The objects in this trail reveal how communities incorporated the buffalo into everyday life, ritual and artistic practice. In Malay material culture, a buffalo-shaped calapa (betel-nut container) brings the animal's associations with patience and abundance into the practice of hospitality. Among prehistoric communities of the region a vessel in the form of a buffalo linked the animal’s strength and agricultural value to a symbol of wealth. 
Across mainland and island Southeast Asia, communities have understood the attributes of the buffalo in different ways while consistently recognizing its importance in daily life, ritual practice and artistic expression. Together, these objects show how shared heritage is created through relationships between people, animals, materials and beliefs. The water buffalo continues to connect these histories across Southeast Asia.

reflection.title: Reflection
reflection.body:
Horses reached Southeast Asia through overland and maritime networks that linked the region with the Middle East, India, China and Mongolia. Communities incorporated them into ceremonial and everyday life and as riding animals, transport, military mounts and participants in processions. Through these many journeys, horses became closely associated with movement, exchange and prestige.
These relationships found expression in artistic and ceremonial traditions across the region. Horse imagery appears in temple reliefs and sculpture from Dvaravati, Angkor and Borobudur, while living traditions such as kuda lumping in Java and pasola in Sumba continue to place the horse at the centre of ritual performance, communal identity and ceremony.
As Hindu-Buddhist traditions spread through trade and migration, they encountered communities where horses already occupied important places in social life. In Buddhist tradition, Prince Siddhartha's horse Kanthaka carried him beyond the palace on the night of his renunciation. With the spread of Islam through the Malay world, the story of the Buraq, the winged steed that carried the Prophet Muhammad during the Night Journey, added another layer of meaning to an animal already associated with movement between earthly and sacred worlds.
The objects in this trail reveal how communities incorporated the horse into everyday life, ritual and artistic practice. A horse-and-rider motif woven into a dastar expresses social standing and physical strength among Indigenous communities in Sabah. Horses also appear on ko-ta boxes carried by Southern Thai fishing communities, where maritime traditions associate them with endurance and companionship. In Nang Talung and Wayang Kulit shadow theatre, horses accompany royal figures in performances that connect storytelling, ritual and community life.
Together, these objects show how communities across Southeast Asia adapted the horse to their own traditions. Moving between roads and rivers, courts and villages, ritual and performance, the horse continues to connect movement, exchange and community across Southeast Asia today.

reflection.title: Reflection
reflection.body:
Deer have inhabited Southeast Asia's forests and woodlands for millennia. Species such as sambar deer, Javan deer, Philippine deer, Visayan Spotted Deer and muntjacs play important ecological roles as seed dispersers and prey. Deer historically formed part of the everyday life of the communities living alongside them through their roles in forest services, subsistence and exchange, and these communities came to admire their grace, speed and vigilance. 
These long relationships gave rise to various tales and diverse cultural traditions. In the Ramayana, Marica disguises himself as a deer of rare beauty to lure Sita into the forest, a story that continues to live through dance drama and puppetry across Southeast Asia. In Buddhist tradition, the Deer Park at Sarnath, where the Buddha delivered his first sermon, became a symbol of peace and learning. As the site of the beginning of Buddhist teaching, it appears in art and architecture from India to Borobudur. Across the Malay world, the mouse-deer — napuh, kancil or pelanduk in Malay — became a clever trickster whose wit triumphs over strength. These traditions connect with wider animal fables that were prevalent across Asia and were reinterpreted by communities throughout Southeast Asia.
The objects in this trail reveal how communities incorporated the deer into artistic, ceremonial and material life. In Kelantanese Malay tradition, the Kijang was admired for its grace, agility and vigilance, qualities associated with leadership and community life. The Kijang motif on coins exchanged between Kelantan and Pattani reflected shared cultural associations. 
Together, these objects show how communities across mainland and island Southeast Asia represented the deer as interpreted through their own beliefs, artistic traditions and everyday practices. Rooted in shared forest environments, the deer continues to connect ecosystems, storytelling and community across Southeast Asia today.

reflection.title: Reflection
reflection.body:
Unlike tigers and leopards, lions are not native to Southeast Asia. Yet for centuries they have occupied an important place in the region's cultural imagination. Artists, patrons and devotees knew the lion through stories, giving rise to stylized and imaginative forms that celebrated the animal's strength, authority and protective qualities.
Communities across Southeast Asia adapted the lion in various ways. In Hindu-Buddhist traditions, it became a guardian placed at the entrances of temples such as Borobudur, Prambanan and Angkor, protecting sacred spaces. Chinese communities incorporated guardian lions into household and ritual life, while Malay communities associated the lion with sacred forces and kingship.
These ideas were reinterpreted through local artistic traditions. Among Batak communities, the singa became a benevolent talismanic figure combining human, water buffalo and crocodile, appearing on houses, amulets and everyday objects. In Malay manuscripts, lions took imaginative forms recalling the gajasimha (elephant-lion), while the Malay Annals placed the lion at the centre of the founding story of Singhapura, where Prince Sang Nila Utama recognized the animal as a sign of an auspicious place.
The objects in this trail reveal how communities gave material form to these diverse understandings. A gold-sheathed betel cutter from Yala reflects interactions between Malay Muslim communities, Theravada Buddhist communities and the Siamese court in a border region. A Chinese ceramic pillow decorated with guardian lions brought protective qualities into the household, while a traditional cloth features the lion as representing royal power and guarding the thresholds between the human and spiritual worlds.
Together, these objects show how communities reimagined the lion through their own beliefs, artistic traditions and material culture. Although the lion never inhabited Southeast Asia's landscapes, it became part of the region's cultural worlds through acts of exchange, creativity and adaptation.

reflection.title: Reflection
reflection.body:
The serpent is native to Southeast Asia, and snakes have inhabited the region for more than 25 million years – far longer than humans. Communities across the region have long venerated serpents as powerful beings closely associated with water, fertility and the forces that sustain life. Moving between land and water and shedding its skin, the serpent embodies renewal, transformation and natural balance.
Within animist cosmologies, the serpent was the lord of the land and water, governing the resources upon which agriculture and communities depended. Curvilinear motifs found on earthenware from Ban Chiang dating to between 300 BCE and 200 CE may be serpentine, reflecting this deep-seated reverence. 
In Hindu cosmology, the serpent coils around Shiva's neck after he swallowed poison to save creation, while in Buddhist tradition, the Naga king Mucalinda shelters the meditating Buddha during a storm. 
As Hindu-Buddhist ideas reached Southeast Asia through networks of trade and exchange some 2,000 years ago, they became intertwined with local beliefs. Across the region, communities came to know the serpent as the Naga (the Great Serpent). The Naga became deeply embedded in folklore, religious narratives, foundation stories and ritual life. 
This is seen in the Khmer origin story, which centres on the marriage between a Brahmin prince and a Naga princess. Similarly, the Sejarah Melayu traces the descent of the founder of Palembang to the Naga. Across the region, traditions attribute the course of the Mekong River to the movements of giant serpents. 
The objects in this trail show how the Naga became part of both ritual and everyday life. At Songkran, water flows through a Naga-shaped flume on a tiered pavilion, making the serpent's association with water part of a communal act of renewal. On painted boat hulls along the Thai-Malay border, the Naga signifies protection and authority. 
Across Southeast Asia, communities reinterpreted the Naga and its enduring relationship with water. Moving between the cosmic and the everyday, the temple and the household, the Naga is an enduring thread in Southeast Asia's shared heritage.

reflection.title: Reflection
reflection.body:
The crocodile is integral to the aquatic ecosystems of rivers, estuaries and coasts across Southeast Asia and has long been part of the lives of the communities who share these waters. As an apex predator, its power and unpredictability inspired stories that reflect both respect and caution. In the Malay world, crocodiles are associated with sacred keramat; in the Hikayat Hang Tuah, a white crocodile appears as an omen during the search for a lost royal crown; while on Timor a local creation story states that the island itself was formed from the body of a crocodile.
Another creature, the makara, has also long been part of the lives of communities across Southeast Asia. Combining the jaws of a crocodile with the body of a fish, the horns of a goat and the trunk of an elephant, the makara brought together qualities drawn from creatures of both land and water. As the vehicle of Hindu river deities such as Ganga, it became associated with the life-giving power of water. Its composite form also made it a guardian of thresholds, and it was placed at temple entrances where it marked the passage between the everyday and the sacred. This creature can be seen at Borobudur in Java and on gold plaques from Óc Eo in Viet Nam and Pyu in Myanmar that date from the fourth to the sixth centuries.
The objects in this trail reveal how communities in Southeast Asia reinterpreted the makara and represented it in various beliefs and practices. A makara palanquin ornament from Pattani was an auspicious accompaniment on circumcision processions for Muslim Malay boys, while a granite makara sculpture from Sungai Mas shows how early communities revered it as a guardian of the thresholds between the everyday and the sacred.
Together, these objects show how communities adapted the makara to express ideas about water, protection, transformation and the crossing of boundaries. Drawing on the natural world while extending beyond it, the makara connects rivers and seas, ritual and everyday life and the many cultural traditions that have shaped Southeast Asia.

reflection.title: Reflection
reflection.body:
Turtles have inhabited Southeast Asia’s rivers, lakes, swamps, mangroves and seas for millennia, and communities across the region have long lived alongside them. Through this longstanding connection, the distinctive forms of turtles became woven into material culture, including as spirit-house figures and motifs for objects that combined beauty, utility and protective meaning. 
Across Southeast Asia, turtles have long been associated with endurance, longevity, protection and the waters that sustain life. Indigenous traditions regarded them as ancient guardians and symbols of environmental balance. These relationships continued as Hindu, Buddhist and Islamic traditions spread through the region via cultural exchange, driven by trade and migration.  
In Hindu tradition, Kurma, the giant turtle and second incarnation of Vishnu, supports the cosmic mountain during the Churning of the Ocean of Milk, making the turtle a symbol of stability and the foundation of the universe. Although turtles are not central figures in Islamic theology, their older associations with longevity, protection and the primordial waters continued through local customs and beliefs.
Across many communities in Southeast Asia, turtles were viewed as creatures that connected different worlds. Living between land and water, they were understood as auspicious in cosmologies in which rivers, seas and wetlands were inhabited by powerful beings. 
Ritual practices helped people negotiate uncertain environments, and the symbolism expressed through turtles enabled people to link everyday experience with broader ideas about balance, continuity and the relationship between people and the natural world.
The objects in this trail reveal how communities expressed the meanings associated with turtles in different ways. Gold plaques placed beneath Khmer temples used the turtle to symbolize stability and longevity, while turtle-shaped lime containers celebrated abundance while reinforcing ideas of protection and endurance. In Peranakan homes, brass ornaments depicting tortoises with cranes drew on Chinese cultural symbolism to express wishes for long life, resilience and harmony. Together, these objects show how turtles connect water, communities and cultural traditions across Southeast Asia, as an enduring part of the region’s shared heritage.

reflection.title: Reflection
reflection.body:
The seas, rivers, lakes, mangroves and floodplains of Southeast Asia historically supported an extraordinary diversity of fish and aquatic mammals that shaped the settlements, food systems, livelihoods and networks of exchange that emerged in the region. Communities living alongside these waters developed rich knowledge of aquatic life and incorporated the behaviours and attributes of the various species into everyday life and ritual. Across Southeast Asia, fish came to embody the life-giving qualities of water, including fertility, abundance and continuity. 
Fish appear across many of the religious and literary traditions that have shaped Southeast Asia. In Hindu tradition, Matsya, the fish incarnation of Vishnu, saves the world, the sacred Vedas and the seeds of life from a cosmic flood. In Cambodian, Thai and Lao retellings of the Ramayana, Suvannamaccha – the golden fish – becomes part of the story of Rama and Hanuman. Taoist traditions tell of the great fish Kun, whose transformation into the bird Peng represents immense potential, while Islamic traditions remember both the great fish Bahamut and the story of the Prophet Yunus as symbols of cosmic order and spiritual reflection.
The objects in this trail reveal how communities historically incorporated fish and other aquatic creatures into material, artistic and ceremonial life. Vietnamese and Thai ceramics were decorated with fish, reflecting their enduring associations. The rare sawfish came to be regarded as a guardian in Thai and Malay traditions, while stingray barbs became weapons, talismans and sacred objects among coastal and seafaring communities. Aquatic mammals occupied sacred roles: whales were revered as protectors along the coast of Viet Nam, while on the island of Lembata in eastern Indonesia whale skulls were venerated at sacred sites. The skeleton of a sperm whale likewise speaks to long relationships between people and the ocean, from veneration to conservation. 
These examples reveal an interconnected maritime world in which trade and exchange led to the circulation of ideas, art and technologies across the region. Together, these objects show how fish and aquatic mammals continue to connect Southeast Asia's waters, communities and shared heritage.

items.title: Neptune Cup Sponge

meta.label: Collection
meta.value: Lee Kong Chian Natural History Museum

meta.label: Caption
meta.value:
The Neptune Cup Sponge (Cliona patera) is shaped like a cup or goblet, growing to over a metre
in both height and diameter — a scale, by some accounts, large enough for a small child to sit inside
its basin. It lives in marine soft sediment habitats across the Indo-West Pacific, with populations
recorded in Singapore, Thailand, and the islands of Koh Rong Sanloem and Koh Koun in Cambodia.
The Neptune Sponge was described by the naturalist Thomas Hardwicke in 1820, thus making it
the first sponge species formally described from the island of Singapore. Its unusual shape and
immense size captured scientific and public attention for the next two centuries.
This specimen in the LKCNHM was collected more than 100 years ago, from a time when the sponge
was still a familiar presence in regional waters. Its elegant goblet-like form and unusual size made
it a coveted museum specimen, fuelling over-collection and rapid decline: abundant in the early 1900s,
it had gone entirely unseen by the late 1900s.
In 2011, two living Neptune Cup Sponges were discovered in the Singapore Straits, within a marine
environment heavily transformed by coastal reclamation. Since then, populations have been found in
various parts of Southeast Asia. In a region where coastal environments are under sustained pressure,
the Neptune Cup Sponge's reappearance in profoundly altered waters is a reminder that the natural
world can still surprise.

reflection.title: Reflection
reflection.body:
For millennia, seashells have connected the coasts, rivers and inland communities of Southeast Asia. Carried far beyond the shores from which they originated, shells circulated as currency and artistic materials for ornaments, furniture and ritual objects. 
Archaeological excavations have uncovered shell motifs and shell beads and bracelets across the region, from early sites in Island Southeast Asia and Timor-Leste to Neolithic and Bronze Age burials on the mainland. Spiral designs inspired by marine snail shells appear on Ban Chiang pottery and Đông Sơn bronze drums, revealing the shell's enduring place in the region's culture since the Bronze Age. Early communities incorporated shells into everyday and ceremonial life. Cowries circulated widely in networks of exchange as monetary tokens and ritual objects, while shell ornaments used in burials expressed identity and social value. 
Across mainland and island Southeast Asia, shells came to be associated with water, life, fertility, health, prestige and knowledge, reflecting close relationships with marine environments and long-standing trade connections between communities.
As shells were transported inland, they acquired new meanings and uses. Communities valued them not only for their beauty and durability but also for the skill required to gather and shape them. In Borneo, Dayak communities fashioned shells into ornaments and prestige objects. With the spread of Hinduism and Buddhism, the shankha (conch shell) acquired additional ritual significance. It became one of the principal attributes of Vishnu, was sounded to begin ceremonies and proclaim victories, and was recognized as one of Buddhism's Eight Auspicious Symbols. In Khmer communities, conch water formed part of ceremonial practice, expressing blessing, purity and legitimacy.
The objects in this trail reveal how communities across Southeast Asia have used shells to express symbolic meanings. From prehistoric ornaments and Đông Sơn drums to Hindu-Buddhist ritual vessels, jewellery, decorations and Peranakan furniture, these objects show how shells were used directly and re-imagined in artistic form across diverse cultural traditions. Together, they reveal seashells as enduring materials of connection, linking coasts and inland communities, everyday life and ceremony, and influencing the many networks that have shaped Southeast Asia's shared heritage.
